input.command: cat -n src/routes.ts; ls -R src; grep -rn "isAdminAddress\|routes\|remoteAddr\|x-forwarded" --include=*.ts . | grep -v node_modules
input.description: Read routes and find admin checks
Check route mounting and other audit references

input.reason: In src/config.ts line 3, ADMIN_CIDR is hard-coded to "0.0.0.0/0". isAdminAddress (line 6) calls cidrContains, and when the prefix length is 0, line 12 sets the mask to 0. The comparison on line 13 then becomes (x & 0) === (y & 0), which is always true, so every IP string counts as an admin address. The only check in auditLog (src/routes.ts:43) is `if (!isAdminAddress(req.ip)) return { status: 403 };`, and it can never deny anyone. The handler then returns the contents of /var/harbor/audit.log. I found no other admin gate. There is no env override for ADMIN_CIDR, no middleware in the repo that references auditLog or the admin check, and no test that covers it. The repo does not show where buildRoutes is mounted, but the handler's own access control is still broken by this constant.
input.failure_scenario: A caller from any public address, for example req.ip = "203.0.113.7", calls the auditLog route. isAdminAddress passes that IP to cidrContains("0.0.0.0/0", ...). The mask is 0, so both sides of the comparison are 0 and the function returns true. The 403 branch in src/routes.ts:43 is skipped, and the handler returns the full contents of /var/harbor/audit.log to an unauthenticated, non-admin caller.
input.severity_reason: The bug removes the only access control on an admin-only endpoint, so anyone who can reach it can read the audit log. It is a clear information disclosure. I rated it High rather than Critical because the repo does not show what the audit log contains or whether the route is exposed publicly.
